At a glance

Best months
  • April to June for breeding birds across the whole country
  • September and October for passage
  • November and February for cranes
Regions
The Camargue and the CrauProvence, the Calanques and the Hyeres salinsLanguedoc, the Aude lagoons and the eastern PyreneesThe Grands Causses and the GorgesThe PyreneesLac du Der and ChampagneThe Chatillonnais and the Forets national parkThe Baie de Somme and the Picardy coastBrittany, the Sept-Iles and OuessantThe Loire estuary, the Briere and Grand-LieuThe Vendee coast and the Marais PoitevinArcachon, Le Teich and the LandesThe Brenne and the SologneThe Alps: the Vanoise, the Ecrins and the MercantourAlsace, the Vosges and the RhineCorsica
Itineraries
The Crane Weekend3 daysThe Brenne Ponds4 daysBrittany and the Sept-Iles6 daysA Camargue Week7 daysThe Atlantic Coast8 daysCorsica End to End8 daysVultures and Mountains10 days
Getting around
A hire car is the honest answer almost everywhere here. The TGV reaches Arles, Strasbourg, Nantes and La Rochelle in under four hours from Paris, and Corsica needs a ferry or a flight

When to Go

France is sixteen regions in three climates, so the right month depends far more on where you go than on the year as a whole. The strip below is a national view; each region card says what its own season is.

Spring

March to June

Everything arrives at once. Herons and terns are back in the Camargue by late March, the Brenne fills with whiskered terns in May, and the Pyrenean and Alpine snowline retreats far enough to walk to by June.

Go for Full song and breeding plumage, and the widest choice of regions of any season.

Trade off The high passes in the Alps and the Pyrenees stay shut into June, so a mountain trip before then is a valley trip.

Typical daily average
  • the Camargue: 6 to 27 °C / 43 to 81 °F
  • Brittany: 5 to 18 °C / 41 to 64 °F
  • Alsace: 3 to 23 °C / 37 to 73 °F
  • the high Alps: -9 to 8 °C / 16 to 46 °F

Summer and autumn

July to October

The mountains open properly in July and August, and from late August the Atlantic coast and the western Pyrenean passes carry the southbound migration.

Go for Alpine and Pyrenean ground at its most reachable, then raptor and crane passage over the Basque passes and waders on the Atlantic bays.

Trade off July and August are the French holiday months, so the coast is busy and rooms cost the most.

Typical daily average
  • the Camargue: 11 to 30 °C / 52 to 86 °F
  • Brittany: 10 to 20 °C / 50 to 68 °F
  • Alsace: 7 to 26 °C / 45 to 79 °F
  • the high Alps: -1 to 13 °C / 30 to 55 °F

Winter

November to February

Cranes fill Champagne, the Camargue holds its flamingos and raptors through the cold, and the Atlantic bays carry their biggest wader counts of the year.

Go for The crane roost at Lac du Der, the cheapest rooms of the year, and a Camargue with nobody on it.

Trade off Eight or nine hours of daylight, and the mountain regions are effectively closed to birding.

Typical daily average
  • the Camargue: 3 to 14 °C / 37 to 57 °F
  • Brittany: 5 to 12 °C / 41 to 54 °F
  • Alsace: 0 to 8 °C / 32 to 46 °F
  • the high Alps: -10 to -1 °C / 14 to 30 °F

3 days

The Crane Weekend

Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG), Lac du Der, Paris

Two hours from Paris and built around two dawns at the roost. November and February are the peaks. This is a self-drive trip rather than an operator product.

  1. Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG)in

  3. 2Etang de la Mer Rouge
  4. 3Etang du Puits

4 days

The Brenne Ponds

Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG), Mezieres-en-Brenne 3 nights, Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG) out

A thousand shallow fish ponds two hours south of Paris, dug in the Middle Ages and still farmed. The Sologne ponds are an hour north of them and work the same way.

  1. Brest (BES)in
  2. 1Reserve naturelle des Sept-Iles
  3. 2Ile d'Ouessant

6 days

Brittany and the Sept-Iles

Brest (BES), Perros-Guirec and the Sept-Iles 2 nights, Ouessant 2 nights, Cap Sizun 1 night, Brest (BES) out

The Sept-Iles boat runs to France's largest seabird reserve, Ouessant is the western rarity island, and the Cap Sizun cliffs hold the mainland colonies between the two.

A Camargue Week

Marseille (MRS) or Nimes, Arles, the delta, the Crau, Arles

The shape almost every operator sells, and the one to copy if you self-drive. One base in or near Arles reaches the lagoons, the salt pans and the steppe without moving hotel.

The Atlantic Coast

Nantes (NTE), the Loire estuary, the Marais Poitevin, Arcachon, Bordeaux

A run down the west coast taking in three of the best wader sites in France and finishing at Le Teich. Best on autumn passage or in mid winter, when the counts are highest.

  1. Bastia (BIA)in
  2. 1Ghisonaccia
  3. 2Corte
  4. 3Calvi
  5. 4Porto-Vecchio

8 days

Corsica End to End

Bastia (BIA), the eastern lagoons, Corte, the Vergio pass, Ajaccio

The island's two endemics live in the high pine forest and the lagoons on the east coast add flamingo and Audouin's Gull, so the trip runs coast to mountain and back.

  1. Toulouse (TLS)in
  2. 1Millau
  3. 2Le Rozier
  4. 3Gavarnie
  5. 4Cauterets

10 days

Vultures and Mountains

Toulouse (TLS), the Grands Causses, the Pyrenees, Toulouse

Four vulture species over the causses, then the high Pyrenean valleys for Lammergeier, Wallcreeper and the alpine list. June to September, once the passes are open.

The Camargue and the Crau

Lagoon, salt pan and stony steppe in the Rhone delta, an hour from Marseille

The delta where the Rhone reaches the Mediterranean is the single most productive place to bird in France, and the one every operator above routes through. Brackish lagoons, salt pans and reed hold flamingos, herons and terns, and the dry Crau steppe just east of it holds a different list again on the same day.

  • Habitat: Brackish lagoon, sansouire and working saltpan across the Rhône delta, with the Crau's dry stone steppe of 11,500 ha of coussous on the plain to its east.
  • When: April and May for the breeding lagoons and the Crau's steppe birds, and the flamingos are on the Étang de Fangassier all year. Autumn passage runs August to October.
  • Getting there: Arles is the base. Much of the Crau is fenced by military and industrial land, so buy the Peau-de-Meau permit at the Écomusée de la Crau in Saint-Martin-de-Crau and take the D24 southwest.
  • Look for: Greater Flamingo, Slender-billed Gull, Little Bustard, Pin-tailed Sandgrouse, Squacco Heron, Collared Pratincole
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional de Camargue (regional park), Reserve naturelle nationale de Camargue (national nature reserve), Reserve naturelle nationale des Coussouls de Crau (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • Parc ornithologique de Pont de Gau : A private reserve with made paths and hides through lagoon and reed, and the surest close view of flamingos in France. It opens daily and charges entry.
    • : The great central lagoon of the delta, and the core of the national nature reserve. The road along its eastern shore gives the view rather than a way in.
    • : The reserve's own information centre on the east shore of the Vaccares. A short trail and hides look over freshwater marsh.
    • : Former salt workings inside the national nature reserve, on permit only from La Capeliere. Hides look over shallow pools.
    • : The sea wall between the lagoons and the beach, walked or cycled. Salt pans lie on one side and the sea on the other.
    • : Reed, wet grazing and open water east of the delta, with marked trails and a tower. Bitterns and harriers hold it.
    • Coussouls de Crau National Nature Reserve : The stony steppe east of the delta, sheep-grazed and the last of its kind in western Europe. It is the ground for Little Bustard, sandgrouse and Lesser Kestrel.
    • : The salt-pan lagoon where France's flamingos breed, on an island built for them. The dike keeps watchers at a distance that leaves the colony settled.
  • Visitor centres: La Capeliere information centre, Musee de la Camargue, Arles
  • Also covers: Coussouls de Crau National Nature Reserve, Digue a la Mer, Etang de Vaccares, Etang du Fangassier, La Capeliere information centre, Le Sambuc, Marais du Vigueirat, Musee de la Camargue, Arles, Parc naturel regional de Camargue, Parc ornithologique de Pont de Gau, Reserve naturelle nationale de Camargue, Reserve naturelle nationale des Coussouls de Crau, Saint-Martin-de-Crau, Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer, Salin de Badon, Salin-de-Giraud
  • Also watch for: Camargue horses and black bulls are worked on the delta and are part of what keeps the marsh open. Beavers are back on the Rhone arms, and the salt pans carry huge numbers of dragonflies from May.

Provence, the Calanques and the Hyeres salins

White limestone sea cliffs and worked salt pans between Marseille and the Iles d'Hyeres

Two national parks sit within an hour of each other on this coast and they do entirely different work. The Calanques are limestone inlets and offshore islands where Bonelli's Eagle nests within sight of Marseille and the Riou archipelago carries the shearwater and storm petrel colonies. Ninety minutes east, the old salt pans at Hyeres are a Ramsar wetland of pans, dunes and a tombolo, and Port-Cros protects the islands beyond them. The Camargue is the bigger name on this coast, and this is the stretch of it that holds the breeding seabirds.

  • Habitat: Two salt-pan systems six kilometres apart on and beside the Giens double tombolo. They mix sansouire and coastal pine with lake and mudflat of varying salinity.
  • When: Spring and summer bring the warm-lagoon species, and a different northern set replaces them through autumn and winter. Access is controlled to keep disturbance down.
  • Getting there: Hyères lies east of Toulon. The Salins des Pesquiers sit on the Giens peninsula road and the Vieux Salins are signposted east of the town, both with marked paths and hides.
  • Look for: Bonelli's Eagle, Scopoli's Shearwater, European Storm Petrel, Eurasian Eagle-Owl, Blue Rock Thrush, Greater Flamingo, Pied Avocet, Audouin's Gull
  • Parks and reserves: Parc national des Calanques, Parc national de Port-Cros, Reserve naturelle nationale de la Plaine des Maures (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • Salin des Pesquiers : A worked salt pan on the Giens tombolo, on the tracks around its edge. Around 350 species are recorded across the Hyeres salins on 900 hectares, and flamingos hold the water all year.
    • Vieux Salins d'Hyeres : The older and larger of the two Hyeres salt pans, east of the town, with a free marked path and screens. Stilts and avocets arrive from March.
    • : The double sand bar running out to the Giens headland. The salt pan sits between its two arms, and the point gives a sea watch.
    • Ile de Port-Cros : The wooded island at the heart of France's first marine national park, by ferry from Hyeres or Le Lavandou. Marked paths cross it and no cars are allowed.
    • Ile de Porquerolles : The largest of the Iles d'Hyeres, part of the same national park, with salt pans, pine and cliff on the south shore. Ferries run from La Tour Fondue.
    • Archipel de Riou : The seabird islands south of Marseille, inside the Calanques national park and closed to landing in the breeding season. A boat or the cliffs above Callelongue give the view.
    • Calanque de Sugiton : The usual way into the park on the Marseille side, on foot from the Luminy campus gate. Summer access is by permit and the number is capped.
    • : The highest sea cliff in France, on the Route des Cretes above Cassis. Alpine Swift and Blue Rock Thrush hold the face and the sea watch is below.
    • : The four islands off the Vieux-Port, in the national park, on the year-round passenger boat. Scopoli's Shearwater breeds here and on Riou.
    • Les Alpilles : A limestone ridge between Arles and Saint-Remy. Bonelli's eagle and Eurasian eagle-owl hold the garrigue.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Parc national de Port-Cros, Hyeres, Maison du Parc national des Calanques, Marseille
  • Also covers: Archipel de Riou, Calanque de Sugiton, Cap Canaille, Cassis, Ile de Porquerolles, Ile de Port-Cros, Iles du Frioul, La Londe-les-Maures, Les Alpilles, Maison du Parc national de Port-Cros, Hyeres, Maison du Parc national des Calanques, Marseille, Presqu'ile de Giens, Reserve naturelle nationale de la Plaine des Maures, Salin des Pesquiers, Vieux Salins d'Hyeres
  • Also watch for: Yelkouan Shearwater breeds on the Riou islands and has no card in the guide yet, so it is named here in prose rather than linked. Bottlenose dolphins and striped dolphins work the water off the Calanques, and the Port-Cros seagrass meadows are the reason the marine reserve exists.

Languedoc, the Aude lagoons and the eastern Pyrenees

Coastal lagoon, garrigue and the Mediterranean end of the Pyrenees, an hour from Perpignan

Where the Pyrenees run into the Mediterranean, a chain of coastal lagoons carries flamingos, gulls and terns within sight of mountains that hold Wallcreeper. Two operators sell this ground as its own week, and it answers a different question from the high Pyrenees three hundred kilometres west.

  • Habitat: A chain of shallow saline lagoons behind the coast, the Étang de Canet alone 480 ha and reed-fringed, backed by the limestone garrigue of the Massif de la Clape.
  • When: Flamingos are on Canet through most of the year and peak as they disperse from the Camargue and the Ebro after breeding. Spring passage brings the pratincoles and Red-throated Pipits.
  • Getting there: From Perpignan take the D611 to Canet-en-Roussillon and the D811 south, which runs beside the lagoon. The northern part is private, and the reserve is walked from Saint-Nazaire.
  • Look for: Greater Flamingo, Audouin's Gull, Purple Swamphen, Slender-billed Gull, Moustached Warbler, European Bee-eater
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional de la Narbonnaise en Mediterranee (regional park), Parc naturel regional des Pyrenees catalanes (regional park)
  • Stops:
    • : A shallow coastal lagoon south of Perpignan, with a reserve, a path and reed beds. Flamingos, terns and Moustached Warbler use it.
    • : A large brackish lagoon behind the coast. The road and the tracks between the oyster beds give the views.
    • : The biggest of the Aude lagoons, inside the regional park. Viewpoints sit at Bages and Peyriac-de-Mer.
    • : A dry limestone massif between Narbonne and the sea. It is Bonelli's Eagle country, with warblers in the garrigue.
    • : A narrow gorge in the Corbieres below the Cathar castles. Alpine Swift, Crag Martin and raptors work the airspace overhead.
    • : The eastern Pyrenean reserve above the Tech valley. It runs forest to alpine and is the closest high ground to the coast.
    • : The mountain that stands over Roussillon, on a track from Vernet-les-Bains. It carries the eastern Pyrenean list.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Parc, Sigean
  • Also covers: Canet-en-Roussillon, Carcassonne, Etang de Bages-Sigean, Etang de Canet-Saint-Nazaire, Etang de Leucate, Gorges de Galamus, Maison du Parc, Sigean, Massif de la Clape, Massif du Canigou, Narbonne, Parc naturel regional de la Narbonnaise en Mediterranee, Parc naturel regional des Pyrenees catalanes, Reserve naturelle de Prats-de-Mollo-la-Preste
  • Also watch for: The Corbières garrigue, the low aromatic scrub of limestone country, carries Hermann's tortoise and Montpellier snake, and the lagoons are among the best French ground for dragonflies.

The Grands Causses and the Gorges

Limestone plateau and gorge in the southern Massif Central, two hours from Montpellier

Four species of vulture fly over one set of gorges here, which is true almost nowhere else in Europe. Griffons were brought back to the Gorges de la Jonte in the early 1980s and Cinereous followed a decade later, and the plateau between the gorges is open sheep country with its own list.

  • Habitat: Limestone plateau of grassland, scattered bush and conifer plantation between the Jonte and Tarn gorges, whose cliffs hold the reintroduced vultures.
  • When: Spring and early summer for the steppe birds of the causse. The vultures are on the cliffs all year and the Belvédère des Vautours reads them from March.
  • Getting there: From the Belvédère des Vautours take the D996 east to Le Truel, then climb to the plateau at Saint-Pierre-des-Tripiers and on to La Parade. Minor roads work the open ground.
  • Look for: Griffon Vulture, Cinereous Vulture, Egyptian Vulture, Bearded Vulture, Short-toed Snake Eagle, Ortolan Bunting
  • Parks and reserves: Parc national des Cevennes, Parc naturel regional des Grands Causses (regional park)
  • Stops:
    • Belvedere des Vautours : The vulture centre above the Gorges de la Jonte, with a viewpoint straight into the colony and a live nest camera. It is the single best vulture watchpoint in France.
    • : The road along the gorge floor between Le Rozier and Meyrueis. Pull-ins sit under the cliffs the vultures use.
    • : The deeper gorge to the north. It holds the same birds with more traffic, and Crag Martin and Alpine Swift work over the villages.
    • : The high plateau between the two gorges, open sheep-grazed limestone. Ortolan Bunting, Tawny Pipit and Short-toed Lark hold the tracks.
    • : The plateau south of the Jonte, quieter than the Mejean. Le Rozier is the way in.
    • : A meander cut deep into the causse south of Millau. Raptors work along the rim.
  • Visitor centres: Maison des Vautours, Le Truel
  • Also covers: Belvedere des Vautours, Causse Mejean, Causse Noir, Cirque de Navacelles, Gorges de la Jonte, Gorges du Tarn, La Cavalerie, Le Rozier, Maison des Vautours, Le Truel, Meyrueis, Millau, Parc national des Cevennes, Parc naturel regional des Grands Causses, Sainte-Enimie
  • Also watch for: Przewalski's horses are kept on the Causse Mejean, and the plateau carries orchids through May and June.

The Pyrenees

High mountain, cirque and forest along the Spanish border, two hours from Pau or Toulouse

The French side of the range is where a first Lammergeier is realistic, and the walk to a cirque puts Wallcreeper, Alpine Accentor and Citril Finch on the same morning. Two national park valleys carry most of the birding: Ossau in the west and Gavarnie in the centre.

  • Habitat: Rocky outcrop, high peak, alpine meadow and mountain lake, with beech and fir on the lower slopes and the Gavarnie cirque walled at 1,500 m.
  • When: June to November is when the high ground is reachable without special equipment, and early July is the best of it for Ptarmigan, Snowfinch and Wallcreeper.
  • Getting there: Gavarnie is at the end of the D923 south of Luz-Saint-Sauveur. Cauterets and the Pont d'Espagne road are the other main way in, and the passes open with the thaw.
  • Look for: Bearded Vulture, Wallcreeper, Alpine Accentor, Citril Finch, White-winged Snowfinch, Rock Ptarmigan
  • National park: Parc national des Pyrenees
  • Stops:
    • : The great amphitheatre at the head of the valley, about an hour and a half on foot from the village. Wallcreeper holds the walls and vultures cross the rim.
    • : A paid car park above Cauterets and the start of the walk to the Lac de Gaube. Forest runs below and alpine above, with Citril Finch on the treeline.
    • : The pass at the head of the Ossau valley on the Spanish border. High open ground opens out at the road end.
    • : A high road pass between the Ossau and Azun valleys. Alpine meadow and cliff run either side.
    • Falaise aux Vautours, Aste-Beon : A griffon colony in the Ossau valley. A visitor centre carries cameras into the nests.
    • : The western national park valley, forest to alpine within an hour's drive. It is the classic route for Lammergeier.
    • : A Basque country pass on the western edge, staffed from July to November. It is one of the great autumn raptor and crane watchpoints in Europe.
  • Visitor centres: Falaise aux Vautours visitor centre, Aste-Beon
  • Also covers: Aulus-les-Bains, Cauterets, Cirque de Gavarnie, Col d'Aubisque, Col d'Organbidexka, Col du Pourtalet, Falaise aux Vautours visitor centre, Aste-Beon, Falaise aux Vautours, Aste-Beon, Gedre, Laruns, Luz-Saint-Sauveur, Parc national des Pyrenees, Pont d'Espagne, Vallee d'Ossau
  • Also watch for: Izard, the Pyrenean chamois, is common in the national park, and marmots whistle from the scree above every valley head.

Lac du Der and Champagne

A very large reservoir in flat farmland, two hours east of Paris

The crane migration through Champagne is the biggest wildlife spectacle in northern France, and Lac du Der is where it stops. Birds roost on the drawn-down reservoir and fly out to the stubbles at dawn, and the same water holds White-tailed Eagle and thousands of duck through the winter.

  • Habitat: A 4,800 ha reservoir built to hold the Marne floods, ringed by drowned oak, with the Étang de la Horre and the Forêt d'Orient lakes on the same clay plain.
  • When: Cranes stage here from late October into December and again in February, with tens of thousands roosting on the water. Winter also brings the White-tailed Eagles.
  • Getting there: Saint-Dizier is the nearest town, two hours east of Paris. The Ferme aux Grues and the Champaubert church are the two roost viewpoints, both signed off the lakeside road.
  • Look for: Common Crane, White-tailed Eagle, Greylag Goose, Great Egret, Osprey, Black Woodpecker
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional de la Foret d'Orient (regional park), Reserve naturelle nationale de l'Etang de la Horre (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : The reservoir itself. A ring of signed viewpoints gives the watching, and the water is drawn down through autumn, which is what creates the roost.
    • : A crane observation site in the fields west of the lake, staffed in season. The birds feed here after leaving the roost.
    • : A peninsula viewpoint on the south shore. It is one of the standard dawn fly-out watchpoints.
    • : A shallow national nature reserve pool south of the lake, quieter than the main water. Reed and marsh birds hold it.
    • : One of the Aube forest lakes south of the Der, inside the regional park. It carries the same birds and far fewer people.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Lac du Der, Sainte-Marie-du-Lac-Nuisement
  • Also covers: Champaubert-aux-Bois, Ferme aux Grues, Giffaumont-Champaubert, Lac du Der-Chantecoq, Lac du Temple, Maison du Lac du Der, Sainte-Marie-du-Lac-Nuisement, Outines, Parc naturel regional de la Foret d'Orient, Reserve naturelle nationale de l'Etang de la Horre, Saint-Dizier, Vitry-le-Francois
  • Also watch for: The oak forest around the lake is old and wet, and beavers work the feeder streams.

The Chatillonnais and the Forets national park

Beech and oak plateau on the Champagne and Burgundy border, three hours south-east of Paris

France's eleventh national park was declared in 2019 and is the first anywhere in the country for lowland broadleaf forest rather than mountain or coast. Three massifs of beech and oak run across the Champagne and Burgundy border on limestone plateau, cut by narrow valleys and dotted with about a hundred tufa marshes. Six pairs of Black Stork breed here, against seventy to ninety in the whole of France, and the park carries the largest integral forest reserve in metropolitan France at 3,087 hectares.

  • Habitat: Continuous beech and oak on Burgundian limestone, with an integral reserve where the forest is left entirely to itself, and open plateau clearings between.
  • When: Spring, when the six woodpeckers are calling and drumming, and the Black Stork and Honey Buzzard are back. The forest is quiet and dark by high summer.
  • Getting there: The D928 and D996 cross the massif from Châtillon-sur-Seine and Arc-en-Barrois. The Maison de la Forêt at Leuglay holds the maps and the reserve is walked from marked car parks.
  • Look for: Black Stork, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Grey-headed Woodpecker, Black Woodpecker, Red Kite, European Honey Buzzard
  • National park: Parc national de forets
  • Stops:
    • Foret domaniale d'Arc-en-Barrois : The Haute-Marne massif, run from the village of Arc-en-Barrois that it surrounds. Three woodpecker species breed in the old stands. OpenStreetMap carries no boundary for the forest itself, so the coordinate here is the village.
    • Abbaye du Val des Choues : A twelfth century abbey deep inside the Chatillon massif at Villiers-le-Duc, open to visitors. It is the readiest way into the Cote-d'Or half of the park, with forest on every side.
    • Reserve integrale de la foret d'Arc-Chateauvillain : 3,087 hectares left entirely to themselves since December 2021, the largest of its kind in metropolitan France. It is a research reserve rather than a visit, and access is regulated.
    • Abbaye d'Auberive : A Cistercian abbey in the Aube valley at the southeast corner of the park. The Black Stork ringing work is run from the village.
    • : A resurgence spring rising at the foot of a cliff in the middle of Chatillon-sur-Seine. It is the easiest introduction to the limestone hydrology the whole park sits on.
    • : A walled medieval deer park on the edge of the village, open and free. Fallow deer hold the inside and the forest edge birds work along its wall.
  • Visitor centres:
    • Maison du Parc national de forets, Chateauvillain
    • Maison de la Foret, Leuglay, The park's interpretation centre on the Burgundy side. It carries the forest ecology displays and the walk information for the Chatillon massif.
  • Also covers: Abbaye d'Auberive, Abbaye du Val des Choues, Chatillon-sur-Seine, Foret domaniale d'Arc-en-Barrois, Maison de la Foret, Leuglay, Maison du Parc national de forets, Chateauvillain, Parc aux daims de Chateauvillain, Reserve integrale de la foret d'Arc-Chateauvillain, Source de la Douix
  • Also watch for: Red deer, roe deer and wild boar are the reason much of this forest was kept, and the rut at Chateauvillain is the set piece of the autumn. European wildcat holds across the massifs. The park has some of the darkest skies in France, which is worth an evening for owls and nightjar as much as for stars.

The Baie de Somme and the Picardy coast

Tidal bay, dune and saltmarsh, two hours north of Paris

The Somme estuary is the largest tidal bay on the French Channel coast and the closest serious wader ground to Paris. The Marquenterre reserve behind the dunes gives made paths and hides, and the bay itself fills and empties on a big tide that pushes birds within reach.

  • Habitat: A 70 km² estuary of sand, mud and saltmarsh, called mollières locally, backed by dune, pine and the reserve pools and hides at the Marquenterre.
  • When: Autumn, and October above all, when the waders concentrate on the Banc de l'Ilette at high tide. Lapwings display over the wet meadows from March.
  • Getting there: The Marquenterre entrance is at Saint-Quentin-en-Tourmont, signed off the D204 north of Le Crotoy. The tide floods fast across the bay, so stay on the dunes and the embankments.
  • Look for: Pied Avocet, Eurasian Spoonbill, Bar-tailed Godwit, Kentish Plover, Common Shelduck, Bluethroat
  • Parks and reserves: Reserve naturelle nationale de la Baie de Somme (national nature reserve), Parc naturel marin des estuaires picards et de la mer d'Opale (marine park)
  • Stops:
    • Parc du Marquenterre : A reserve of lagoon, dune and pine behind the bay, with three marked circuits and staffed hides. Spoonbill and heron colonies nest here.
    • : The estuary itself. The sea walls at Le Crotoy and Saint-Valery give the view on a rising tide.
    • : The national nature reserve covering the northern bay. The Marquenterre is the visitable part of it.
    • : Shingle, pools and rough grazing at the southern end of the bay. It is free to walk and good for passage.
    • : A low headland at Saint-Valery. It looks across the channel of the bay.
  • Visitor centres: Maison de la Baie de Somme, Lanchères
  • Also covers: Cap Hornu, Cayeux-sur-Mer, Hable d'Ault, Le Crotoy, Maison de la Baie de Somme, Lanchères, Parc du Marquenterre, Parc naturel marin des estuaires picards et de la mer d'Opale, Reserve naturelle de la Baie de Somme, Reserve naturelle nationale de la Baie de Somme, Rue, Saint-Valery-sur-Somme
  • Also watch for: Harbour and grey seals haul out on the sandbanks in the middle of the bay and are visible from the shore at low water.

Brittany, the Sept-Iles and Ouessant

Seabird island, granite headland and estuary, four hours west of Paris by train

France's seabirds are concentrated on a handful of Breton islands, and the Sept-Iles holds the country's only gannet colony along with puffins and auks. Out at the western tip, Ouessant is the French rarity island, and its autumn does what Fair Isle does for Britain.

  • Habitat: Granite islands and stacks off the Côte de Granit Rose carrying France's only Gannet colony, and a low heath and small-valley island 20 km out in the Atlantic.
  • When: The Sept-Îles colonies run April to July. Ouessant is an autumn island: September and October for the seawatch off Créac'h, and October for the passerine falls.
  • Getting there: Boats to the Sept-Îles leave Perros-Guirec. Ouessant is a ferry from Le Conquet or a daily flight from Brest, and the island is best worked by hired bicycle.
  • Look for: Northern Gannet, Atlantic Puffin, Razorbill, Common Murre, European Storm Petrel, Red-billed Chough
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel marin d'Iroise (marine park), Parc naturel regional d'Armorique (regional park), Reserve naturelle nationale des Sept-Iles (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • Reserve naturelle des Sept-Iles : The seabird islands off Perros-Guirec, worked by boat from the harbour. Landing is only on Ile aux Moines, and the gannets and auks are watched from the water.
    • : The westernmost French island, by ferry from Le Conquet or Brest. Autumn brings seabird passage off the headlands and rarities into the gardens.
    • Cap Sizun reserve : An LPO cliff reserve west of Douarnenez, with a marked path along the seabird ledges. April to July is the window.
    • : The classic Breton headland at the end of the Cap Sizun. An onshore wind turns it into a seabird watchpoint.
    • : A high headland on the Crozon peninsula and another seabird passage station. Chough holds the cliff grass.
    • : A shingle bar with lagoons behind it along the south side of the Cap Sizun. Waders and passage birds use it.
  • Visitor centres: Station LPO de l'Ile-Grande
  • Also covers: Baie d'Audierne, Camaret-sur-Mer, Cap Sizun reserve, Ile d'Ouessant, Le Conquet, Parc naturel marin d'Iroise, Parc naturel regional d'Armorique, Perros-Guirec, Pointe de Pen-Hir, Pointe du Raz, Reserve naturelle des Sept-Iles, Reserve naturelle nationale des Sept-Iles, Station LPO de l'Ile-Grande
  • Also watch for: Grey seals breed on the Sept-Iles and in the Iroise, and the Iroise sea is one of the few French waters with resident bottlenose dolphins.

The Loire estuary, the Briere and Grand-Lieu

Marsh, reed and shallow lake around Nantes, two hours from Paris by train

Three different wetlands sit within an hour of Nantes: the salt pans at Guerande, the reed and open water of the Briere, and Lac de Grand-Lieu, which is the largest natural lowland lake in France in winter and holds a heron colony that is nationally important.

  • Habitat: A 6,300 ha shallow lake that doubles in area when it floods. Reed, willow carr and floating vegetation fringe it, with the Briere marshes and the Guerande salt-pans beside it.
  • When: Spring, when the heronry is at its fullest and the lake is high. Winter brings the wildfowl and the lake is at its most extensive.
  • Getting there: The Maison du Lac at Bouaye is 15 km southwest of Nantes and holds the only public views of Grand-Lieu, which is otherwise a closed reserve. Guérande and Brière are further west.
  • Look for: Purple Heron, Eurasian Spoonbill, Whiskered Tern, Bluethroat, Black-winged Stilt, Eurasian Bittern
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Parc naturel regional de Briere (regional park), The marsh north of Saint-Nazaire. The canal paths and the causeways at Saint-Lyphard and Saint-Andre-des-Eaux give the views.
    • Reserve naturelle nationale du Lac de Grand-Lieu (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : A shallow lake southwest of Nantes whose core is closed. The observatory at Passay and the LPO site at Saint-Philbert give the views.
    • Maison du Lac de Grand-Lieu : The interpretation centre on the north shore. A tower looks over the reed.
    • : Working salt pans between Guerande and Le Croisic, on the tracks between the basins. Waders and terns use the pans and Bluethroat holds the samphire.
    • : A seabird watchpoint on the north side of the estuary mouth.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Lac de Grand-Lieu, Bouaye
  • Also covers: Batz-sur-Mer, La Baule, Maison du Lac de Grand-Lieu, Bouaye, Marais salants de Guerande, Parc naturel regional de Briere, Pointe de Chemoulin, Reserve naturelle du Lac de Grand-Lieu, Reserve naturelle nationale du Lac de Grand-Lieu, Saint-Nazaire, Saint-Philbert-de-Grand-Lieu
  • Also watch for: Coypu are everywhere in the Briere canals, and the salt pans at Guerande are still worked by hand.

The Vendee coast and the Marais Poitevin

Mudflat, wet meadow and canal marsh on the Atlantic coast, south of Nantes

The Baie de l'Aiguillon is one of the two or three most important wader sites in France, and the wet meadows and canals of the Marais Poitevin behind it hold a breeding list that has largely gone from the rest of lowland Europe. La Rochelle is the base, and every site is within an hour of it.

  • Habitat: The Baie de l'Aiguillon's mudflats at the mouth of the Sèvre Niortaise, with wet meadow and pollarded ash canals inland and the Île de Ré salt-pans to the west.
  • When: Winter for the waders and Brent on the bay, spring for the breeding waders and terns on the wet meadows, and the whole passage in between.
  • Getting there: La Rochelle is the airport and rail head. Saint-Denis-du-Payre is signed off the D746 and Lilleau des Niges is at Les Portes-en-Ré at the north end of the island.
  • Look for: Black-tailed Godwit, Pied Avocet, Whiskered Tern, Bluethroat, Little Bustard, Eurasian Curlew
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional du Marais poitevin (regional park), Reserve naturelle nationale de la baie de l'Aiguillon (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : The mudflats at the head of the Anse de l'Aiguillon. The sea wall at Esnandes and the pointe de l'Aiguillon give the view on a rising tide.
    • : A wet-meadow reserve with a staffed observatory. It is one of the best places in France to see breeding waders at close range.
    • : The canal marsh inland of the bay. The paths around Coulon and Arcais give the views.
    • Reserve naturelle de Lilleau des Niges : Former salt pans at the northern tip of the Ile de Re. The LPO reserve has a path and hides.
    • : Saltmarsh and lagoon south of Rochefort. The LPO reserve has a long trail and hides over the flats.
    • : A sand spit at the mouth of the Lay. The national nature reserve is watched from its landward edge.
    • : A small reserve on Noirmoutier at the estuary's southern edge. Terns and gulls nest in the colony.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Marais poitevin, Coulon
  • Also covers: La Rochelle, Le Chateau-d'Oleron, Les Portes-en-Re, Lucon, Maison du Marais poitevin, Coulon, Noirmoutier-en-l'Ile, Parc naturel regional du Marais poitevin, Pointe d'Arcay, Reserve naturelle de la Baie de l'Aiguillon, Reserve naturelle de Lilleau des Niges, Reserve naturelle de Moeze-Oleron, Reserve naturelle de Saint-Denis-du-Payre, Reserve naturelle des marais de Mullembourg, Reserve naturelle nationale de la baie de l'Aiguillon
  • Also watch for: Otters use the Marais Poitevin canals, and the wet meadows carry Fritillary in April.

Arcachon, Le Teich and the Landes

Tidal basin, lagoon reserve and pine forest, an hour from Bordeaux

The Bassin d'Arcachon is a tidal basin with a wader reserve built into the delta of the Leyre, and the Parc ornithologique du Teich is the easiest place in south-west France to see spoonbills and waders from a hide. Behind it, the Landes pine forest runs south for a hundred kilometres.

  • Habitat: A huge tidal basin of mudflat and eelgrass, with 400 ha of former salt-pans at Audenge, the Leyre delta reserve at Le Teich, and pine and heath across the Landes behind.
  • When: Autumn and winter for the waders and wildfowl on the basin. The Teich reserve works in every month and the Banc d'Arguin holds its tern colony through summer.
  • Getting there: Le Teich is signed off the A660 at the head of the basin, 50 km from Bordeaux, and the reserve trail is six kilometres of hides. Audenge is on the northern shore road.
  • Look for: Eurasian Spoonbill, Pied Avocet, Osprey, Bluethroat, Dartford Warbler, European Nightjar
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional des Landes de Gascogne (regional park), Reserve naturelle nationale du banc d'Arguin (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : A shifting sandbank at the mouth of the basin holding a Sandwich Tern colony. Boats run from Arcachon, and the Dune du Pilat gives the overview.
    • : Former fish ponds on the east side of the basin, with paths along the dikes. Far fewer visitors come here than to Le Teich.
    • : The wooded channels above the reserve. Marked paths run out from Le Teich.
    • : The great dune south of Arcachon. It gives the overview of the banc d'Arguin and the basin mouth.
  • Visitor centres:
    • Parc ornithologique du Teich, A reserve of lagoons and reed in the Leyre delta, with a long circuit and twenty hides. It opens daily, charges entry, and anchors the whole region.
  • Also covers: Arcachon, Delta de la Leyre, Domaine de Certes et Graveyron, Dune du Pilat, La Teste-de-Buch, Le Teich, Mimizan, Parc naturel regional des Landes de Gascogne, Parc ornithologique du Teich, Reserve naturelle du Banc d'Arguin, Reserve naturelle nationale du banc d'Arguin
  • Also watch for: The Dune du Pilat, the tallest sand dune in Europe, sits at the mouth of the basin and is worth an hour for the view over the banc d'Arguin.

The Brenne and the Sologne

Thousands of shallow fish ponds in central France, two hours south of Paris

The Brenne is a landscape of man-made fish ponds, more than two thousand of them, and it holds a breeding list that includes Whiskered Tern, Purple Heron and Black-necked Grebe in numbers that matter nationally. The Sologne to the north is the same idea under oak and heath, and quieter.

  • Habitat: More than a thousand shallow fish ponds in a clay basin, reed-fringed and heath-edged, with the Sologne's own pond and forest country to the north.
  • When: Spring and summer, when the heron and egret colonies are active. Winter fills the larger étangs with duck, and Black-necked Grebe is on La Gabrière from spring.
  • Getting there: The D17 south of Mézières-en-Brenne threads the ponds with roadside parking at each. The Chérine reserve has the hides, and guided visits reach parts otherwise closed.
  • Look for: Whiskered Tern, Purple Heron, Black-necked Grebe, Eurasian Bittern, Savi's Warbler, European Honey Buzzard
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional de la Brenne (regional park), Reserve naturelle nationale de Cherine (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • Reserve naturelle de Cherine : The core reserve of the Brenne, free to enter, with four hides on marked paths and a nature house.
    • : One of the Cherine reserve's ponds. Its hide gives the closest whiskered tern watching in France.
    • : The largest pond in the Brenne. Its causeway gives the view.
    • : A large Sologne pond in oak and heath country. A road runs along one side.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Parc, Rosnay
  • Also covers: Etang de la Mer Rouge, Etang du Puits, Etang Massse, Le Blanc, Maison du Parc, Rosnay, Mezieres-en-Brenne, Parc naturel regional de la Brenne, Reserve naturelle de Cherine, Reserve naturelle nationale de Cherine, Romorantin-Lanthenay
  • Also watch for: European Pond Terrapin is native here and basks on the pond margins from April, which is unusual enough in France to be worth looking for.

The Alps: the Vanoise, the Ecrins and the Mercantour

High alpine meadow, larch forest and rock, two hours from Grenoble or Nice

Three national parks hold the French alpine list, and a cable car or a high road pass puts you into it without a mountaineering day. Bearded Vulture was reintroduced to the Alps from the 1980s and is now seen regularly in all three, and the Mercantour above Nice adds Mediterranean species to the alpine ones.

  • Habitat: Larch and arolla pine to the tree line, then alpine pasture, moraine and rock up to the glaciers, with the Mercantour's Mediterranean valleys on the southern flank.
  • When: Late June to early September, once the high passes open. The Iseran and the Lautaret are usually clear by late June and close again with the first snow.
  • Getting there: The Col de l'Iseran road climbs from Bourg-Saint-Maurice and the Col du Lautaret from Briançon. Plan du Lac is walked from above Termignon in the Vanoise.
  • Look for: Bearded Vulture, Rock Ptarmigan, Black Grouse, White-winged Snowfinch, Alpine Accentor, Wallcreeper
  • National parks: Parc national de la Vanoise, Parc national des Ecrins, Parc national du Mercantour
  • Stops:
    • : The highest paved pass in the Alps, above Bonneval-sur-Arc in the Vanoise. Snowfinch and accentor work the ground around the car park.
    • : A road-end viewpoint high in the Vanoise above Termignon. It looks across the Doron to the glaciers, ibex hold the slopes and alpine birds work the car park.
    • : A pass between the Ecrins and the Brianconnais, with an alpine botanic garden and easy high ground either side.
    • : The Mercantour valley above Nice. The Alpha wolf park sits at Saint-Martin, and forest runs to alpine within half an hour.
    • : A high Mercantour valley of rock and lake, a full day on foot. Ptarmigan and accentor hold the summit ridges.
    • : A walk up from Bourg-d'Arud into the Ecrins, through forest to a lake under the crags.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Parc national de la Vanoise, Pralognan
  • Also covers: Bonneval-sur-Arc, Briancon, Col de l'Iseran, Col du Lautaret, Lac du Lauvitel, Le Bourg-d'Oisans, Maison du Parc national de la Vanoise, Pralognan, Parc national des Ecrins, Parc national du Mercantour, Plan du Lac, above Termignon, Pralognan-la-Vanoise, Saint-Martin-Vesubie, Vallee de la Vesubie, Vallee des Merveilles
  • Also watch for: Ibex were saved in the Vanoise and are now easy there, and wolves recolonised France through the Mercantour in 1992.

Alsace, the Vosges and the Rhine

Riverine forest, sandstone ridge and mountain, north-east on the German border

The Rhine floodplain forest, the Ried wet meadows and the Vosges ridge sit within an hour of Strasbourg, and between them they carry the French woodpecker list almost complete. White Stork was down to a handful of Alsatian pairs in the 1970s and is now on village roofs across the plain.

  • Habitat: Flooded Rhine woodland with standing dead trees grading into rich meadow and forest, with the Ried de Sélestat's wet grassland and the Vosges sandstone above.
  • When: Spring for the six woodpeckers and the breeding herons, autumn for the passage and the tit flocks, and winter for the duck on the Rhine reservoirs.
  • Getting there: The Rohrschollen island is reached from Strasbourg's southern industrial port road. Cars are barred from the canal-side track and parts close in the breeding season.
  • Look for: White Stork, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Black Woodpecker, Grey-headed Woodpecker, Hazel Grouse, Red Kite
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Parc naturel regional des Vosges du Nord (regional park), The sandstone and beech country in the north, a UNESCO biosphere reserve. It carries the French woodpecker list.
    • Parc naturel regional des Ballons des Vosges (regional park)
  • Stops:
    • : Rhine floodplain forest on an island in the river, inside the Strasbourg city limits, with marked paths.
    • : Riverine forest and backwater where the Sauer meets the Rhine in the far north of Alsace.
    • : Wet meadow along the Ill south of Selestat. The landscape has largely gone elsewhere on the plain.
    • : A high point on the main Vosges ridge above Munster. A road runs up to it, and it holds the alpine-edge species of the range.
    • : Old Rhine channels and reed at the Swiss corner, with a ringing station and marked trails.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Parc des Vosges du Nord, La Petite-Pierre
  • Also covers: Colmar, Le Hohneck, Maison du Parc des Vosges du Nord, La Petite-Pierre, Munchhausen, Munster, Parc naturel regional des Ballons des Vosges, Parc naturel regional des Vosges du Nord, Petite Camargue Alsacienne, Reserve naturelle de l'ile du Rohrschollen, Reserve naturelle du Delta de la Sauer, Ried de Sélestat, Saint-Louis, Strasbourg
  • Also watch for: Lynx and, more recently, wolf are back in the Vosges, and the sandstone ridge in the north carries chamois that were introduced in the 1950s.

Corsica

Mountain, maquis, the dense evergreen scrub of the Mediterranean, and coastal lagoon, a ferry or a short flight from the mainland

Corsica is where the French list picks up birds that are on it nowhere else. The Corsican Nuthatch lives only in the island's laricio pine forest, the Corsican Finch is shared with Sardinia alone, and the coastal lagoons on the east side add flamingo and Audouin's Gull to a mountain trip.

  • Habitat: Laricio pine forest above beech in the Aïtone and Valdo-Niello valleys, low maquis on the southern limestone, and the reed-fringed Étang de Biguglia on the east coast.
  • When: April to June for the mountain forest, when the Corsican Nuthatch and Citril Finch are in song. Biguglia holds waders and wildfowl through passage and winter.
  • Getting there: The D84 crosses the island through Aïtone and over the Col de Vergio from Porto to Corte. Biguglia is south of Bastia beside the N193 with a reserve centre at the north end.
  • Look for: Corsican Nuthatch, Corsican Finch, Marmora's Warbler, Audouin's Gull, Red Kite, Moltoni's Warbler
  • Parks and reserves: Parc naturel regional de Corse (regional park), Reserve naturelle des Bouches de Bonifacio (national nature reserve), Reserve naturelle de l'etang de Biguglia (national nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : Laricio pine forest above Evisa, the classic and most reliable site for Corsican Nuthatch. The forest road gives the watching.
    • : The highest road pass on the island, between the Aitone and Valdo-Niello forests. Nuthatch and Citril Finch hold the pines, with alpine ground above.
    • : The other great pine forest, on the Calacuccia side of the Vergio pass.
    • : The largest Corsican lagoon, just south of Bastia. The nature reserve holds flamingos and waders, with Moustached Warbler in the reed.
    • : A quieter east-coast lagoon behind the beach. Audouin's Gull works offshore.
    • : The road up from Corte into the central massif, forest to high lake. Red Kite crosses the valley and Alpine Chough holds the summit ridges.
    • : The white cliffs at the southern tip. Shearwater passage runs through the strait and Blue Rock Thrush holds the rock.
  • Visitor centres: Maison du Parc naturel regional de Corse, Corte
  • Also covers: Calvi, Col de Vergio, Etang de Palo, Falaises de Bonifacio, Foret d'Aitone, Foret de Valdo-Niello, Ghisonaccia, Maison du Parc naturel regional de Corse, Corte, Porto-Vecchio, Reserve naturelle de l'etang de Biguglia, Reserve naturelle des Bouches de Bonifacio, Restonica valley
  • Also watch for: The mouflon is native here and lives in the high central massif, and the island has its own subspecies of red deer, brought back from Sardinian stock after it went extinct in the 1960s.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in France?

April to June if you want one trip to cover the country, because that is when the lowland regions are in full song and the mountains are opening. September and October for passage on the Atlantic coast and over the western Pyrenean passes. November and February for the crane roost at Lac du Der.

Where should I go for a first French birding trip?

The Camargue. It has the widest list in the shortest drive, it works in every month of the year, and it is the region every operator sells, so there is more written about it than anywhere else in France. Base yourself in or near Arles and you can reach the lagoons, the salt pans and the Crau steppe without changing hotel.

Do I need a car?

For most of the regions above, yes. The reserves sit outside the towns and rural bus services are thin. The exceptions are the Camargue, where Arles is on the TGV and there are guided day trips from it, and Alsace, where Strasbourg's trams and regional trains reach the Rhine forest. Corsica needs a car once you are off the boat.

Which French birds can I see nowhere else?

One: the Corsican Nuthatch, which needs the mature laricio pine of the Corsican mountains. The Corsican Finch is shared only with Sardinia. Everything else on the French list is shared with a neighbour, which is what makes France a country of regions rather than of endemics.

Where do I see all four European vultures in a day?

The Gorges de la Jonte in the Grands Causses. Griffon, Cinereous, Egyptian and Bearded Vulture all fly over the same gorge, which is true of very few places in Europe. The Belvedere des Vautours above the gorge is free to look from and has a live camera into a nest.

Is the Camargue worth it in winter?

Yes, and it is the cheapest and emptiest time to go. The flamingos stay, the raptor list is at its best, and the Crau holds wintering Little Bustard. What you lose is the breeding herons and terns, which arrive from March.

Can I see Lammergeier in France?

Yes, in two places. The Pyrenees carry the native population and are the more reliable of the two; the Alpine birds descend from releases that began in the 1980s and are seen regularly in the Vanoise, the Ecrins and the Mercantour. Both are watched from valley heads and road passes.

What about France's overseas departements?

They each deserve a page of their own, and this one stays metropolitan. French Guiana, Reunion, Guadeloupe, Martinique and Mayotte hold avifaunas with their own families, their own seasons and their own endemics, and French Guiana in particular is a serious Neotropical destination that would be buried as a paragraph here.

How much does a French birding trip cost?

Accommodation is the largest line and France is a mid-priced European country for it. A guided operator week runs to several thousand dollars; the same ground self-driven costs a fraction of that, and most of the reserves above are free or charge a small entry.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, France has 29 local bird clubs across 13 regions. See every French club by region.

LPO BirdLife in France, and the manager of many of the reserves above including the Sept-Iles and Moeze-Oleron. Visit Bretagne Vivante The Breton nature society, which runs the Cap Sizun reserve and much of the seabird monitoring. Visit Tour du Valat The Camargue research institute, and the source behind most published flamingo and wetland figures. Visit Reserves naturelles de France The network body for the national nature reserves, with a searchable list of every one. Visit Faune-France The national participatory recording portal, run by LPO and the regional associations. Visit
